extracted.intended_audience: professional mathematicians and advanced students interested in plane geometry and conic sections
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic construction and characterization of the greatest ellipse inscribed in, and the least ellipse circumscribed about, a given quadrilateral; includes tangency conditions, equations for coefficients, selection criteria for admissible roots, and geometric corollaries (locus of centres, existence/uniqueness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation form for an ellipse inscribed in a quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: An ellipse inscribed in quadrilateral PQRS (with sides given by linear equations) may be written in the central-form a(y — k)^2 + 2b(x — h)(y — k) + c(x — h)^2 + ... = 1 (equation (5) in the paper).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use coordinates with axes parallel to two sides through a corner P; denote centre (h,k) and coefficients a,b,c (and cross-term/offset constants). This is the starting parametrization to impose tangency to the four sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangency conditions for an inscribed ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: The four sides being tangents to the ellipse impose four algebraic relations among a,b,c,h,k and the side parameters (equations (13)–(16)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly: (b^ — ac)(a — h m) = a(...), (b'^ — ac)(β — kf) = c(...), etc. (see text). These must be satisfied to ensure the conic is tangent to each side (or its prolongation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Area extremum condition for inscribed ellipse (objective)
rubrics_metrics.description: The area of an inscribed ellipse (product of principal semi-axes) is expressible in terms of the coefficients; to find the greatest inscribed ellipse one maximizes this area.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After eliminating variables, the squared principal semi-axes satisfy a quadratic whose constant term equals the product of their squares; maximizing area reduces to minimizing the combination (ac − b^2). (Text: 'Hence, ac — b^2 must be a minimum (12)'.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reality condition for ellipse (ac − b^2 > 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For the conic to be an ellipse with real area the combination ac − b^2 must be positive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any candidate solution (roots for h,k,a,b,c) that yields ac − b^2 ≤ 0 gives an imaginary or non-elliptic conic and must be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locus of centres of conics tangent to the sides
rubrics_metrics.description: All conic sections that touch the sides (or sides produced) of a given quadrilateral have their centres situated on a fixed straight line which bisects the diagonals of the quadrilateral (equation (19) and subsequent remark).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equation (19) (in the paper) expresses the condition on the centre (h,k); geometrically this line is the bisector of the diagonals PR and QS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection criterion among algebraic roots for inscribed ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic elimination leads to multiple algebraic roots; the admissible root is the one producing positive ac − b^2 and corresponding to a maximum of the area (the other root may give an imaginary area or a minimum/hyperbola).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper analyzes two roots (one yields expression (21) which is negative — rejected; the other (22) is positive and accepted). Always check sign of derived expressions and that they make ac − b^2 positive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equation form for a conic through four vertices (circumscribed about quadrilateral)
rubrics_metrics.description: All conics passing through P,Q,R,S (circumscribing the quadrilateral) can be written in general quadratic form a x^2 + 2b x y + c y^2 + 2d y + 2e x + 1 = 0 with the coefficients linked by four linear relations determined by the four points (equations (26)–(30)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the intersection of diagonals for axes (as recommended) to simplify; the linear relations (27)–(30) fix most coefficients up to a free parameter (b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective for least circumscribed ellipse (minimization)
rubrics_metrics.description: The least circumscribed ellipse is obtained by minimizing the quantity related to the product of the squares of the principal semi-axes (equivalently an expression involving a,c,b — the paper indicates the expression containing ac − b^2 must be minimized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting the differential of that expression to zero with respect to the free parameter b leads to a cubic equation (equation (33)) whose admissible root gives the required circumscribed ellipse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algebraic equation determining parameter b for least circumscribed ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: The minimization condition for the circumscribed problem produces a cubic equation in b (equation (33)), whose real roots must be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solve the cubic; only roots that make ac − b^2 positive and produce an actual ellipse are admissible. The paper observes typically one admissible root among possibly three real roots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniqueness/existence selection rule for circumscribed ellipse
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytically there may appear up to three algebraic solutions for the circumscribed minimal ellipse, but only those giving ac − b^2 > 0 and hence a genuine ellipse satisfy the geometric problem; typically only one does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check signs and ellipse-definiteness; discard roots corresponding to hyperbolas or imaginary areas as Euler and the author remark.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geometric corollary: bisector property (centres on diagonal-bisector)
rubrics_metrics.description: Corollary: the centres of all conic sections tangent to the sides (or sides produced) of a quadrilateral lie on the straight line which bisects the diagonals of the quadrilateral (derived from (19)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives a simple geometric locus test for candidate centres and can be used to reduce unknowns when searching for inscribed or circumscribed conics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical existence criterion via auxiliary circle intersection (constructive problems)
rubrics_metrics.description: In constructive problems (e.g., building a triangle from given sum of two sides and an inscribed circle), the paper repeatedly uses the existence criterion: the auxiliary circle (or constructed locus) must meet a given line in two, one or no points, giving respectively two, one or no admissible geometric solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When converting an existence question to an intersection of loci (circles, arcs), check whether intersection count matches expected number of solutions and treat tangency (single intersection) as unique solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extremal (differential) conditions to find principal axes
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal semi-axes of a central conic are maxima/minima of the radius r; equate differential of r^2 under constraint of the conic equation to zero to obtain the quadratic (e.g., equation (11)) whose roots are squares of principal semi-axes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method yields an equation whose constant term equals the product of squared semi-axes and underlies the area expressions used in the maximization/minimization problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification step: check whether derived coefficients yield real tangents to given sides
rubrics_metrics.description: After solving algebraic equations for a,b,c,h,k (or for b in circumscribed case), verify that the resulting conic is tangent to the given four lines/points (signs, orientation) and yields the intended geometric configuration (salient vs re-entrant quadrilateral cases discussed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper separates 'salient' quadrilaterals (inscribed ellipse exists) from 're-entrant' ones (ellipse form changes sign). Always substitute back into tangency relations (13)–(16) and the conic equation to confirm.
